title: Hypoglycemia
summary: Hypoglycemia means glucose is below the person’s safe range. Symptoms can include sweating, shaking, hunger or confusion.
why: The brain needs glucose. A person may lose the ability to recognise a low or treat it independently.
how: Insulin can outlast a meal or activity can increase glucose use. Fast-acting carbohydrate is used for a low when the person is awake and can swallow safely. Rechecking is part of the treatment plan.
example: Someone feels shaky during a walk, stops in a safe place and uses their low-glucose plan.
caution: If someone cannot swallow safely, give nothing by mouth. Use prescribed glucagon if available and call emergency services. Review repeated lows with the care team.
question: Is a severe low defined only by a number?
answer: Severity also depends on needing another person’s help because thinking or physical function is impaired.

title: Hypoglycemia unawareness
summary: With impaired awareness, the usual early warnings of a low may be faint or absent.
why: A person can still converse or feel well while glucose is falling to an unsafe level.
how: Repeated lows can shift when the body releases warning hormones. A specialist can help develop a plan to reduce exposure to lows.
example: A partner notices confusion before the person feels the tremor they usually associate with a low.
caution: Discuss missing warnings and recurring lows promptly. CGM alarms can help, but a sensor may lag or lose signal.
question: Can symptoms alone confirm recovery?
answer: A recovery check is important even when symptoms improve. Use your agreed monitoring plan.

title: Hyperglycemia
summary: Hyperglycemia is glucose above the person’s target range. Thirst, frequent urination and fatigue can accompany a sustained rise.
why: A high after lunch has different possible causes from a high that persists through illness.
how: Less insulin than needed, infection, stress hormones or a delivery interruption can leave more glucose in the bloodstream.
example: A pump user feeling unwell checks the delivery system and follows their team’s ketone-testing plan.
caution: A high with vomiting, ketones or rapid breathing needs urgent assessment. Glucose alone cannot exclude ketoacidosis.
question: Can glucose rise without eating?
answer: Yes. The liver releases glucose, especially during illness or stress.

title: Dawn phenomenon
summary: The dawn phenomenon is an early-morning rise in glucose as the body prepares to wake.
why: The waking value alone cannot tell you whether glucose was steady, falling or already rising overnight.
how: Hormonal changes can increase liver glucose output and reduce insulin sensitivity towards morning.
example: A learner compares several overnight traces and notices glucose stayed steady until the hours before waking.
caution: Late meals, missed insulin and overnight lows can look similar by morning. Review patterns before changing basal insulin.
question: Which part of the trace is most informative?
answer: The period before the rise, together with meal timing, activity and insulin records.
takeaways: Bring context to a basal review

title: Somogyi effect
summary: The Somogyi effect is a proposed rebound high after an overnight low. Evidence is weak for it as a common explanation of fasting highs.
why: Assuming a rebound from a single high can obscure an actual overnight low or a dawn rise.
how: Counter-regulatory hormones can respond to a low, but morning hyperglycemia does not establish that sequence. Overnight CGM or planned checks provide context.
example: Two people wake at the same glucose. Only one example trace includes a low earlier in the night.
caution: A compression-related sensor low is another possibility. Confirm unexpected readings according to device instructions.
question: Does a high at breakfast prove there was a low overnight?
answer: No. Look for evidence of the low itself and discuss recurring patterns with the team.
takeaways: A morning high cannot prove a rebound
Look for evidence of a preceding low

title: Honeymoon phase
summary: Partial remission is a temporary period after diagnosis when some pancreatic beta cells still make insulin.
why: Insulin needs can change quite quickly, which can feel confusing after learning an initial routine.
how: As metabolic stress settles, remaining cells may provide more insulin for a time. The autoimmune process can continue.
example: A child needs less insulin than shortly after diagnosis and the family brings the new pattern to the clinic.
caution: Do not stop insulin independently. The duration and degree of remission vary, and ending remission is not a personal failure.
question: Does partial remission mean the diagnosis was mistaken?
answer: No. Residual insulin production can occur in type 1 diabetes.

title: Glucagon and counter-regulatory hormones
summary: Glucagon signals the liver to release glucose. Adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone also help the body respond to falling glucose or stress.
why: These signals help explain why a sprint or a frightening event can produce a rise even without food.
how: The liver can release stored glucose and make new glucose. In T1D, the usual glucagon response to a low may be impaired.
example: Before a race, a runner notices a rise despite eating the same breakfast as on a training day.
caution: A hormone explanation cannot diagnose the cause of an individual reading. Severe lows still require emergency action.
question: Is emergency glucagon the same thing as insulin?
answer: No. Rescue glucagon raises glucose through the liver; insulin lowers circulating glucose.
takeaways: Rescue glucagon has a distinct role

title: Stress, sleep and illness
summary: Stress, disrupted sleep, illness and menstrual-cycle changes can alter glucose independently of food.
why: Recording a few days of context may explain why a familiar plan gives different results.
how: Cortisol and adrenaline can increase liver glucose output. Infection can increase insulin resistance; reduced appetite during illness may pull glucose the other way.
example: A student compares glucose during exams with a quieter week and notes shorter sleep.
caution: Do not attribute illness or ketones to stress alone. Seek help using your sick-day plan.
question: Does everyone see the same change around a period?
answer: No. Patterns vary between people and sometimes between cycles.
takeaways: Treat illness as a separate safety issue
